title: The skeptical judge
summary: Give the full science fair talk with your board, brief an AI to cross-examine you like a fair but skeptical judge, and adopt one improvement on the spot.
materials: your board draft from this week's Build
the family AI assistant, with a grown-up nearby
an index card for fair catches

steps.title: A talk with a spine, and a judge who pokes it
steps.body:
The science fair talk is the easiest talk you will ever structure, because the board already is the structure: question, plan, trials, result. Say it in that order and the talk builds itself. Open with the person and the problem, so the room knows why the build exists before it knows what the build is. Close with the result and the one thing you would do next. Aim it at two minutes.

Now the judge. A real fair has one, and here is the secret nobody tells kids: the skeptical judge is not your enemy. Skeptical is a compliment. It means your claims are worth checking, which is week 1's oldest lesson, test it or trust it, pointed at you for a change. A judge's question finds the thinnest panel of your board while the fix still costs nothing. Tonight you rent that judge before the fair does it for real.

The twist: the AI plays the judge, and the judge is only as good as its briefing. Week 6 taught you the recipe, job, facts, limits. Tonight that skill stops being an exercise and starts being a tool you reach for.

And carry the question of the week in your pocket: is it ever good to fail in public? You are about to arrange a small public failure on purpose, in front of your family, so a bigger one cannot happen at the fair. Every fair catch that lands on your index card tonight is a hole in your project found out loud, with people watching, and part of you will wish it had turned up quietly instead. The trouble is that quietly, on your own, it probably would not have turned up at all. The family in the seats and the judge you briefed are the reason the thin panel shows itself while there is still time.

And then the ring. Tonight's motion is 'It is better to fail in front of people than alone', three rounds, either side, and you steelman the other side before you answer it. Tonight hands you exhibits for both sides, so argue the one you actually believe rather than the one that looks easier to win. Your recording still ends on your own answer.

steps.title: Brief your judge
steps.body:
Write the ask before you open the assistant, the week 6 way.

The job: you are a science fair judge, fair but skeptical. Ask me one question at a time about my project, three questions in all, and do not answer them for me. After my third answer, tell me in one sentence which part of my project sounded thinnest.

The facts: read your board to the machine. The question, the plan, the trials and the result, a few sentences each, including the wall that fell and the one improvement. A judge briefed only on your topic will ask fog; a judge briefed on your actual claims will ask exactly where it hurts, which is what you are paying it for.

The limits: only ask about things I claimed. Wait for my answer before the next question. Keep each question to two sentences.

Read the whole ask to a grown-up before sending it, the season's rule, same as always. Then, before facing the judge, run the talk once alone against the timer: board beside you, two minutes, no stopping to fix anything. If it runs long, mark what to trim; trimming is the rehearsal working.
checklist: My ask names the job, the facts and the limits, and a grown-up heard it before I sent it
The facts part carries my actual question, plan, trials and result, not just my topic
I ran the full talk once against the timer without stopping
It landed inside two minutes, or the thing to trim is marked

steps.title: Face the judge
steps.body:
Family in their seats, board standing, you standing beside it, never behind it. Give the whole talk first, top to bottom, no interruptions.

Then the cross-examination: three questions from the AI judge, read out loud by a grown-up so the room hears what you hear. Answer each one the debate way, claim, reason, example, and pull every example from something real: a bug diary line, a stumble from the real test, a number on the budget sheet. A judge can smell a made-up example from across the gym.

When a question lands on something your board does not answer, and one will, do not bluff. Say, that is a fair catch, and write it on the index card. A scientist who says I do not know yet, here is how I would find out, beats a scientist who improvises an answer, every single time, at every fair on earth.

After the third answer, collect the judge's one sentence about your thinnest panel. Now adopt one improvement on the spot, before the glow fades: move a photo, reword a heading, add the missing number, rehearse a better answer. Say it out loud in one line, I am changing this because the judge showed me that, and make the change to the board or the talk right now.
checklist: I gave the whole talk standing at the board before any questions came
Every answer carried a claim, a reason and a real example from my log, trials or budget
Every fair catch went on the index card instead of getting a bluff
One improvement went into the board or the talk immediately, named in one line

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the improved talk from the top, board in frame. Keep recording: say the judge's hardest question and give your best answer to it. Close with the question of the week: is it ever good to fail in public? Use tonight as your evidence, whichever way you answer.
